title: What are the bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`) and the shift operators — `<<` (left shift), `>>` (arithmetic/signed right shift, preserves sign), and `>>>` (logical/unsigned right shift, fills with 0) — and why does `>>>` matter for treating an `int`/`long` as unsigned bits?
shortTitle: What are the bitwise and shift operators?

s1_definition.profdef: The bitwise operators work on the individual binary digits of integer types: `&` is bitwise AND, `|` is bitwise OR, `^` is bitwise exclusive-OR, and `~` is bitwise complement that flips every bit. The shift operators move bits left or right: `<<` shifts left filling with zeros, equivalent to multiplying by powers of two; `>>` is the arithmetic or signed right shift that preserves the sign by filling the vacated high bits with copies of the sign bit; and `>>>` is the logical or unsigned right shift that always fills the vacated high bits with zeros. The `>>>` operator matters because Java's integer types are signed, so when you need to treat an int or long as a pure bit pattern or an unsigned value, `>>>` gives the correct zero-filled result where `>>` would propagate a one from a negative number's sign bit.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine account flags and codes at National Bank of India stored as rows of on-off switches. Bitwise AND keeps only the switches both rows have on, OR turns on any switch either row has on, exclusive-OR turns on switches that differ, and complement flips every switch. Shifting left is like sliding all the switches one position toward the high end, which doubles the value, and shifting right slides them toward the low end. The subtle part is the right shift: the signed version copies the leftmost switch, which marks positive or negative, into the new gaps, while the unsigned version always puts fresh off switches into the gaps. When a code is really just a pattern of switches rather than a signed amount, you must use the unsigned shift so a leftmost on switch does not flood the gaps with ones.
s1_definition.oneliner: &, |, ^, ~ manipulate bits; << multiplies by two, >> shifts right keeping the sign, and >>> shifts right filling zeros, which is essential for treating signed int/long as unsigned bit patterns.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The bitwise operators work on the individual binary digits of integer types: `&` is bitwise AND, `|` is bitwise OR, `^` is bitwise exclusive-OR, and `~` is bitwise complement that flips every bit. The shift operators move bits left or right: `<<` shifts left filling with zeros, equivalent to multiplying by powers of two; `>>` is the arithmetic or signed right shift that preserves the sign by filling the vacated high bits with copies of the sign bit; and `>>>` is the logical or unsigned right shift that always fills the vacated high bits with zeros. The `>>>` operator matters because Java's integer types are signed, so when you need to treat an int or long as a pure bit pattern or an unsigned value, `>>>` gives the correct zero-filled result where `>>` would propagate a one from a negative number's sign bit.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine account flags and codes at National Bank of India stored as rows of on-off switches. Bitwise AND keeps only the switches both rows have on, OR turns on any switch either row has on, exclusive-OR turns on switches that differ, and complement flips every switch. Shifting left is like sliding all the switches one position toward the high end, which doubles the value, and shifting right slides them toward the low end. The subtle part is the right shift: the signed version copies the leftmost switch, which marks positive or negative, into the new gaps, while the unsigned version always puts fresh off switches into the gaps. When a code is really just a pattern of switches rather than a signed amount, you must use the unsigned shift so a leftmost on switch does not flood the gaps with ones.

**One line to remember:** &, |, ^, ~ manipulate bits; << multiplies by two, >> shifts right keeping the sign, and >>> shifts right filling zeros, which is essential for treating signed int/long as unsigned bit patterns.

sections.s2_technical:
Integer types in Java are stored as fixed-width two's-complement binary: int is thirty-two bits and long is sixty-four bits, and the highest bit is the sign bit, where zero means non-negative and one means negative. The bitwise and shift operators act directly on these bits, which is why they are the foundation of flag manipulation, masks, hashing, compression, and low-level protocol handling.

The four bitwise operators combine bits position by position. The AND operator, a single ampersand, produces a one in a position only when both operands have a one there, which you use to test or mask bits, for example value AND a mask isolates selected bits. The OR operator, a single pipe, produces a one when either operand has a one, which you use to set bits, for example combining feature flags. The exclusive-OR operator, a caret, produces a one when the two bits differ, which you use to toggle bits and in checksums and simple hashing, and a useful identity is that XOR with the same value twice returns the original. The complement operator, a tilde, is unary and flips every bit, turning each zero to one and one to zero, and because of two's complement, the complement of a number equals negative that number minus one.

The shift operators move the whole bit pattern. The left shift, a double less-than, moves bits toward the high end and fills the vacated low bits with zeros, and each single left shift multiplies the value by two, so shifting left by n multiplies by two to the n, which is a fast way to compute powers of two and to build bit masks like one shifted left by three. The signed right shift, a double greater-than, moves bits toward the low end and fills the vacated high bits with copies of the sign bit, which preserves the number's sign and effectively divides a signed value by two rounding toward negative infinity. For a positive number the vacated bits fill with zero, but for a negative number they fill with one, keeping it negative.

The unsigned right shift, a triple greater-than, also moves bits toward the low end but always fills the vacated high bits with zeros regardless of the sign bit. This is the key operator for treating a value as an unsigned bit pattern. Because Java has no unsigned int or long type, when you hold a value whose high bit is set and you want to interpret the full pattern as a large non-negative number rather than a negative signed number, you must shift with the triple greater-than so the sign bit does not propagate. A classic example is extracting the high half of a value, or computing a midpoint index safely: the well-known binary-search midpoint written as low plus high divided by two can overflow into a negative number for large indices, and the robust form uses the unsigned right shift on the sum so the result stays correct. Another is reading bytes from a larger word, where you shift right and mask, and the shift must be unsigned so a high byte with its top bit set is not sign-extended. The signed right shift on a negative number fills with ones and would corrupt such a pattern, which is precisely the bug the triple greater-than avoids.

The senior-level points are these. Shift amounts are taken modulo the width, so shifting an int by thirty-two is the same as shifting by zero, a common surprise. The operators apply to int and long only, with smaller types promoted to int first, so a byte or short is widened before shifting, and that widening sign-extends, which can reintroduce sign bits you must mask away with an AND against a byte mask. For genuinely unsigned arithmetic Java provides helper methods such as the unsigned divide and compare utilities and the methods that interpret a value as unsigned, which you prefer for clarity. In banking you meet these operators in bit-packed flags, in hashing for sharding keys, in CRC and checksum code, and in binary file and network protocol parsing, where getting signed versus unsigned shifting right is the difference between correct and corrupted data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India packs several account permission flags into a single int to save space in a high-volume table, and it must set, clear, test, and toggle individual flags. This is exactly the domain of the bitwise operators: OR to set, AND with a complement to clear, AND to test, and XOR to toggle.

Problem 2 — A hashing routine that shards accounts across database partitions reads a thirty-two-bit hash and extracts its high bits to pick a shard, but using the signed right shift produced negative shard numbers for hashes with the top bit set, sending records to an invalid partition. This is exactly why the unsigned right shift matters: the hash is a bit pattern, not a signed amount, so the vacated bits must fill with zeros.

Problem 3 — A binary-search over a sorted array of millions of transaction indices computed the midpoint with a plain sum and divide, which overflowed to a negative index for very large bounds. This is exactly the unsigned-right-shift midpoint fix.

We will build a runnable demo with a PermissionFlags class using the four bitwise operators, a Sharder that extracts shard bits with the unsigned right shift and contrasts the buggy signed shift, and a safe binary-search midpoint. The code includes the flags helper, the sharder, and a demo main.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: permission flags, a hash with its top bit set, and large binary-search bounds.

Step 1: Starting from zero flags, the OR operator sets the VIEW and TRANSFER bits, producing the binary pattern with bits zero and one on. Testing TRANSFER with the AND operator returns true because that bit is set.

Step 2: The XOR operator toggles the TRANSFER bit off, because XOR flips a set bit to clear, and testing TRANSFER now returns false. The complement operator on VIEW flips all bits, shown as its binary pattern.

Step 3: The shift basics run. One shifted left by three equals eight, showing left shift multiplies by two to the power three. Negative eight shifted right by one with the signed shift stays negative four, because the sign bit is copied into the vacated position. Negative eight shifted right by twenty-eight with the unsigned shift becomes a positive number, because zeros fill the vacated positions.

Step 4: The sharder extracts the top four bits of a hash whose top bit is set. With the unsigned right shift the vacated bits fill with zeros, so the shard is a valid number between zero and fifteen.

Step 5: With the buggy signed right shift, the sign bit propagates into the vacated high bits, so the extracted value comes out negative, which would select an invalid database partition. This is the concrete bug the unsigned shift avoids.

Step 6: The binary-search midpoint is computed. The naive sum-and-divide overflows the int range for the large bounds and produces a negative index, while the unsigned-right-shift form keeps the sum's bit pattern intact and yields the correct positive midpoint, demonstrating why the unsigned shift is the robust choice.

```
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    After set VIEW|TRANSFER: 11 ; has TRANSFER? true
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    After toggle TRANSFER: 1 ; has TRANSFER? false
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    ~VIEW (complement) = 11111111111111111111111111111110
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    1 << 3 = 8 (multiply by 2^3)
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    -8 >> 1 = -4 (signed: keeps negative)
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    -8 >>> 28 = 15 (unsigned: zero-filled, positive)
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    shardFor (>>>): 9 (valid 0..15)
2026-10-30 18:20:40 WARNING shardForBuggy (>>): -7 (NEGATIVE → invalid partition!)
2026-10-30 18:20:40 INFO    safe midpoint (>>>): 1750000000 ; naive (low+high)/2 = -397483648 (overflowed negative!)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Bitwise on flags int
    set:    flags | FLAG        (OR)
    clear:  flags & ~FLAG       (AND with complement)
    test:   (flags & FLAG) != 0 (AND)
    toggle: flags ^ FLAG        (XOR)

  Shifts
    1 << 3          → 8            (×2^3, zero-fill low)
    -8 >> 1         → -4           (signed: sign bit copied in)
    -8 >>> 28       → 15           (unsigned: zero-fill high)

  Why >>> matters (top bit set hash)
    hash = 0x9ABCDEF0 (negative as signed int)
      >>> 28 → 0x9 = 9 valid shard
      >>  28 → sign-extended → negative invalid partition

  Overflow-safe midpoint: (low + high) >>> 1  keeps bits correct
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Bitwise & Shift Semantics ═══

  ┌─ Rules ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ &  AND (test/mask)   |  OR (set)   ^  XOR (toggle)       │
  │ ~  complement (flip all bits)                           │
  │ << left shift (×2^n, zero-fill low)                     │
  │ >> signed right (sign-extend high bits)                 │
  │ >>> unsigned right (zero-fill high bits)                │
  │ shift amount taken mod 32 (int) / 64 (long)             │
  │ byte/short promoted to int (sign-extends) before shift  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID / Rules ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Rule: hash/pattern → >>> ; signed amount ÷2 → >>         │
  │ S: PermissionFlags = bits; Sharder = routing math       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ PermissionFlags      │        │ Sharder              │
  │ + set/clear/has/toggle│        │ + shardFor (>>>)     │
  └──────────────────────┘        │ + shardForBuggy (>>) │
                                  │ + midpoint (>>>)     │
                                  └──────────────────────┘

  Contract for shardFor(hash):
    Pre:  shardCount is a power of two
    Post: returns 0..shardCount-1 (always non-negative)
    Guarantee: >>> prevents sign-bit propagation
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The bitwise operators act on the individual binary digits of integer types. The AND operator produces a one only where both operands have a one, which you use to test or mask bits. The OR operator produces a one where either operand has a one, which you use to set bits. The exclusive-OR operator produces a one where the two bits differ, which you use to toggle bits and in checksums, and applying it twice with the same value returns the original. The complement operator is unary and flips every bit. These are the foundation of flag packing, masks, hashing, and protocol handling.

The shift operators move the whole bit pattern. The left shift moves bits toward the high end filling zeros, so each shift multiplies by two, which is how you build masks like one shifted left by three. The signed right shift moves bits toward the low end and fills the vacated high bits with copies of the sign bit, preserving the sign and effectively dividing a signed value by two, so a negative number stays negative because the ones propagate. The unsigned right shift also moves bits right but always fills the vacated high bits with zeros regardless of the sign bit.

The unsigned right shift matters precisely because Java's integer types are signed and there is no unsigned int or long. When a value is really a bit pattern or an unsigned quantity rather than a signed amount, and its top bit is set, the signed right shift would propagate that one through the vacated high bits and corrupt the result, while the unsigned shift zero-fills and gives the correct non-negative value. In a project at National Bank of India this caused a real defect: a sharding routine extracted the high bits of a thirty-two-bit account hash to pick a database partition, and because it used the signed right shift, hashes whose top bit was set came out negative and selected an invalid partition. Switching to the unsigned right shift fixed it because the hash is a pattern, not a signed number. We hit the same family of bug in a binary search over millions of transaction indices, where the naive midpoint of sum divided by two overflowed to a negative index for large bounds, and the robust form that shifts the sum right by one with the unsigned shift kept the result correct.

The nuances I always add are that the shift amount is taken modulo the width, so shifting an int by thirty-two is the same as by zero, that smaller types are promoted to int before shifting and that promotion sign-extends so you often mask with an AND against a byte mask to clean up, and that for genuinely unsigned arithmetic Java provides explicit helpers like the unsigned divide and compare methods which I prefer for clarity. So the complete answer is that AND, OR, XOR, and complement manipulate bits, left shift multiplies by two, the signed right shift divides while keeping the sign, and the unsigned right shift zero-fills, which is exactly what you need to treat a signed int or long as an unsigned bit pattern in hashing, sharding, byte extraction, and overflow-safe index math.

keyPoints: << left shift, >> signed right shift, >>> unsigned right shift
>>> matters for negative numbers — fills with 0 instead of sign bit
Common use: flags, permissions, hash functions, low-level protocols
